title: The bathroom flaws that infuriate every designer
text:
The bathroom flaws that infuriate every designer

Throne Room Politics: Inside Designers Obsession with Bathrooms

How one close look at everyday bathroom flaw will permeantly ruin your routine.

I paused, leaving the bathroom. Something strange was happening, but what was it?

There was a woman in a wheelchair who had finished washing her hands. She seemed stuck, but she wasn’t stuck. She kept reaching and reaching, unable to get something, but what couldn’t she get?

“Can I help you?” I mustered up the courage to ask, realizing she must think I’m the most awkward person just staring at this interaction.

“I think” she reached a bit further, “I can get it.” With one large effort, she reached and finally grabbed a paper towel that was just out of reach.

We looked at each other. My curiosity passed, and anger rose in its place.

She smiled meekly. “They put the paper towels just out of reach.”

https://medium.com/media/93c9edb8c5cbea26cdacdae5f39c5153/href

Today, this memory flashed through my mind as I held my daughter up to the sink. We’re in a restaurant bathroom and the sink looms over her. She’s too small to use it and yet there are no stools for her to use. She’s prevented from doing what we tell every child and adult to do: wash your hands for 20 seconds to help prevent the spread of germs.

This problem wasn’t just about hand-washing. It wasn’t just about changing stations or accessible stalls. It wasn’t just about aesthetics or form. It was about gender and cultural norms. It was about making the world a better place. This is why designers are so opinionated on bathrooms.

My bathroom experiences lead me to conclude:

  1. In the United States, we categorize disability and people with children similarly, resulting in experiences that aren’t designed for either. For instance, almost every bathroom in the United States places the changing table in the handicap stall. This funnels women with children and people with disabilities into one stall. If that stall opens when there’s a line and there is someone with a disability or impairment or a someone who needs to a change a diaper, that stall is rarely held for the people who need this stall most.
  2. We use men’s designs for women’s bathrooms, and the one size fits all is a fundamentally flawed paradigm. For instance, when there are changing tables in common areas, such as airports, women use them as a place for their make up. There is no where else in the bathroom that has this much counter space. (This one grossed me out and still does).
  3. Our biases persist even after we’ve identified them; we often aren’t taking action to solve our biases. As an example, we still haven’t eliminated biases from automatic hand washers, which results in people of color having poor experiences while trying to wash their hands. (Bigotry Encoded: Racial Bias in Technology)
  4. We invent new methods to solve problems, but they often don’t solve the problem and/ or create new ones. Take a look at the new handwashing machines that have driers, soap, and faucets all in one. The iconography is confusing and I myself am personally guilty of thinking the dryer icon was the hand washing icon.

Designers have tried to tackle different aspects of the bathrooms but to date in the United States, I haven’t seen an end to end beautiful execution that solves 1–4 of the pain points listed above.

Challenge 1: Many still categorize people with disabilities or impairments the same as people with children, resulting in experiences that aren’t designed for either.

I stood in the bathroom while my 3-year-old held her ears.

“It’s loud, Momma.” She complained, clutching her ears even tighter.

I tuned in to understand her experience. The hand driers were going off. Toilets were flushing loudly. Stall doors were banging as people went in and out. Then, the noise stopped. I reached for my daughter to have her stop covering her ears, then the noises started up again — multiple driers, toilets being flushed, doors banging, people talking.

Bathrooms are loud places and not just for kids.

“Many autistic people find everyday noise too loud, painful or hard to tune out: a 2021 meta-analysis estimated that 41% currently have hyperacusis (sounds are too loud or too painful) and 61% have had it at some point.⁠”
(Source: Dr. Sensory)

As a designer, I have to ask: Does everything need to be so loud?

A simple solution to the hand drier noise is going back to paper towels… but that contributes to more waste in our ecosystem. Hand driers reduce carbon emissions and save trees. In fact, according to Pinnacle, “A typical school using 30 hand dryers will save 17 trees worth of paper towels per year.” We solved one problem to create another. Woof.

The innovation didn’t meet the mark, so let’s keep trying rather than accepting good enough. What if we sought to solve the problem of the loud noises in the bathroom AND our environmental impact? What would we do? Patch the current problem and explore sound reduction options? OR could we think about loud and quiet areas in bathrooms? Could we rethink bathroom acoustics?

Along with loud sounds being normal, in the United States, we’ve accepted the premise that the handicap stall is where the changing station should be. We’ve created a singular, multi-purpose stall.

This has failed anecdotally for me. I have 2 children and brought both of them into the large, single bathroom stall in a restaurant with me. I started changing one daughter on the table while the other went potty. Then, I heard a woman crutch in. Uh oh, I thought. There’s only one stall the person on crutches can use, and I’m in it. I began to panic and as every woman does, I started apologizing even though this was also the stall I should be in. How else was I going to change my kid? The woman ended up waiting over 5 minutes for us. There was nothing that could be done because there was only one stall for us both.

This memory stands in stark contrast to the stalls in Europe in the airport. They decided that the changing stall shouldn’t be stuck in the bathroom stall or confined exclusively to the woman’s bathroom. Men change diapers too. They created a net new space for changing tables that was private and nested between the men and women’s bathrooms.

We can do better once we stop accepting that our current failed paradigm is sufficient. We can have quieter bathrooms. We can have better stalls. We can have better experiences changing our children. It’s not our gear that has failed. It’s our approach.

If we pull the changing stations from the women’s bathrooms, where will women put on their makeup? (great but gross question, my friend)

Challenge 2: Men and women have fundamentally different bathroom needs, and thus require different experiences.

Caroline Criado Perez in her book Invisible Women: Exposing Data Bias in a World Designed for Men notes that women on average take 2.3 times longer in the bathroom than men do. This is due to women’s complex outfits (jumpsuits for instance where the whole outfit must come off), the fact that women are more likely to take their children in the bathroom, and also that mechanically women must sit to use the bathroom. It’s not just the outfits. It’s the desire to use the powder room, but those rooms have fallen out of fashion despite the need still being present.

The powder room came into vogue in the 18th century to fix one’s wig and one’s makeup. This room (now commonly half baths on the first floor) was a room in a convenient location, often featuring a couch where women could collect themselves or converse in privacy with other women. This still happens today, but the mechanisms and who is there are quite different today.

Bathrooms traverse more than male and female lines, more than parent and child; they traverse gender lines. A 2013 report from The Williams Institute UCLA School of Law noted that nearly 70% of transgender people have undergone verbal harassment in bathrooms and 10% have experienced physical assault. Many have tried to tackle this challenge and gender norms at once by making bathrooms for all.

These good intentions have been divisive. Proponents note that privacy is maintained and when everyone is brought together, it can aid in the reduction of negative interactions. It also supports caregivers and those with young children to have a more seamless experience — moms and dads will have equal access to changing stations. Moreover, it reduces costs, as there is now a need for one bathroom rather than 2–3 distinct areas (men, women, family). This is starting to sound like a viable solution. Then, societal and cultural norms start to break down the scalability and make this be the bathroom solution.

Women may find shared spaces more cumbersome to navigate. Ankitha Gattupalli writes in Designing around Debate: The Gender-Neutral Bathroom

Women may feel uncomfortable tidying up in front of the mirror or attending to their menstrual needs in unisex bathrooms…Many religions and cultures prohibit sharing intimate spaces like toilets with unrelated people of the opposite sex. Societal notions around menstruation may also make it difficult for the international spread of the multi-stall gender-neutral bathroom.

Unisex bathrooms are a highly divisive issue, which is why many have looked at another alternative solution: spatial equity v. fixture equity. Jonathan Yeung in his article Spatial Equity in Urban Infrastructures: Public Restrooms Addressing Women’s Needs defines these as: “Spatial equity provides an equal amount of floor area for different genders, while fixture equity ensures an equal number of stalls or fixtures for each.”

Spatial equity is what is most commonly employed — men and women get the same amount of space for the bathroom. For me, the biggest reason this breaks down can be seen at sporting events. I love women’s soccer games and most people who attend are women and children. When spatial equity is applied, this leaves women facing long lines while men don’t have them. Now think about football. These events are overwhelmingly attended by men and there’s a biological reason for that, according to the Times. When spatial equity is applied, the men’s lines are usually longer than womens. You need to apply the right logic at the right time to get the best output OR transition a set of bathrooms to meet the gender who attends. Taylor Swift frequently sells out football arenas and her base is primarily women.

Fixture equity is essentially stating — let’s have the same number of urinals in mens as stalls in women's. This logic starts to break down when men may need the ability to sit down and go. Not every man can stand either, so we’re employing exclusionary design tactics.

We’ve talked about how the current designs aren’t meeting our needs, but we have to ask why? Why are we still deploying known exclusionary and biased practices?

Challenge 3: Our biases persist even after we’ve identified them; we often aren’t taking action to solve our biases.

I honestly wanted to scream as I watched a woman of color try and get the automatic faucet to work. “These never work well,” she said smiling. I recalled why this didn’t work for her. “It’s not you,” I thought. “You are experiencing a biased in technology.”

Taylor Synclair Goethe notes in “Bigotry Encoded: Racial Bias in Technology” why this happens.

The dispenser used near-infrared technology to detect hand motions, an article on Mic read. The invisible light is reflected back from the skin which triggers the sensor. Darker skin tones absorb more light, thus enough light isn’t reflected back to the sensor to activate the soap dispenser. Which means that dark-skinned restroom users will have to skip washing their hands with this not-so-sensitive soap dispenser.

Most of the creators of this technology did not set out to bias or exclude a group. However, they created this technology without a diversity of opinions or perspectives. As Goether continues, “The less diversity there is in a workplace environment, the more likely major design flaws will be present that only affect people of color.”

For me, as I stood there watching this woman struggle to use the faucet, I couldn’t help but think this bias has been known and identified and even viralized on social media. Yet, it still persists.

https://medium.com/media/8a9bf255ea843ccd1603c10de738cf42/href

The most aggravating part to me is that technology companies have solved this problem using radar, ultrasonic or capacitive sensors, but these solutions are more expensive. Add higher cost to biases being dismissed as “glitches” or “unreliable sensor issues” rather than a failure of equity, and you see companies waving aside inclusive technology (Uprooting Bias in Artificial Intelligence).

Right now, many companies are on a trajectory where all roads lead to the bottom line. If it’s not saving dollars, it’s not a company priority. But (shakes fist in the air) we have to do better. We have to stop accepting inequitable experiences as normal. We have to care about the entire human experience, rather than just one subset across age, sex, identity, or race division.

Part 4: We invent new methods to solve problems, but they often don’t solve the problem and/ or create new ones.

Meet the faucet that feels straight out of Wall-E. It is touchless and integrates the soap dispenser and hand drier all in one. Unlike the inventions in Wall-E, this one doesn’t meet the mark.

According to Lila Vaugh in Why Some Automatic Faucets Cause More Complaints Than Manual Faucets,

Touchless faucets were originally introduced to improve hygiene, modernize restroom infrastructure, and reduce water waste. In theory, automatic faucets should create a better user experience than traditional manual fixtures.
Yet in many airports, malls, schools, office buildings, hospitals, and stadiums, facility managers continue receiving frequent complaints about automatic faucet systems — sometimes even more complaints than older manual faucets ever generated.
Users commonly report delayed activation, weak water flow, random shutoffs, false triggering, temperature inconsistency, and confusing operation. In high-traffic public environments, these issues quickly affect restroom satisfaction and building perception.

Enter every designer ever.

I’ve watched and experienced this interaction so many times. The icons are often confusing, and the water icon looks like the dryer, so I’ve started washing my hands by drying them. Then, if the experience doesn’t work, I panic and start waving around like a mad woman. I’m sure there’s a great SNL skit waiting to be made of my behavior interacting with a technology failure. This failure however has an easy solution — the right icons.

For non-designers, one of the principles of iconography is to use universal icons. Examples of these include the magnifying glass for search or the ubiquitous medical cross icon to signifying where to get medical help. All other icons should follow the 7 principles of iconography:

  1. Clarity of meaning
  2. Visual clarity (or readability)
  3. Simplicity
  4. Familiarity
  5. Alignment and balance
  6. Consistency across the board
  7. Personality and branding

And yet (deeply sighs while putting her index and thumb on the bridge on her nose), we have chosen to use conflicting icons in public bathrooms for users. Each bathroom has a new set of icons and faucets to learn. My favorite is when companies must write: “Please turn off faucet” because patrons continuously leave on their manual faucet. We sought for progress. We ended up with a bunch of people waving their hands around fighting with a bias technology.

Conclusion

Now that every designer feels personally seen in their annoyance with bathrooms and every non-designer feels annoyed, let’s talk about what we can do about it. To me, these apply to a lot of design problems, not simply the bathroom.

  1. We have to start designing for the 20% and using ethnographic research (observing people while they complete a task) to create meaningful experiences. If we continue to design for 80% (often the able-bodied community), we will continue to litter biases and inequitable experiences.
  2. Learn from Dr. Seuss. “Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It’s not.” We must stop accepting biased experiences as “normal.” It’s not normal to exclude a group of people. Let the people wash their hands!
  3. Employ best practices with design and AI. Some of these known issues are really simple solves and make the experience so much better, such as choosing the right icon.

P.S.

If this article made you mad, good! We have to care to change our course. I also want you to leave on a positive note, so please enjoy one piece of humor I stumbled upon while researching this topic.

https://medium.com/media/1519393d32399eeab361aee194aae265/href

The bathroom flaws that infuriate every designer was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: In-system design: from code to Figma and back. Prototyping in your real design system
text:
In-system design: from code to Figma and back. Prototyping in your real design system

In-System Design 3/3

A practical guide for designers: why I stopped choosing between canvas and code, and how one prototype travels both ways.

For designers who know Figma well and have never written production code, and for the design system teams around them. Every technical word is explained in the box at the end.

I have a confession that does not go down well on LinkedIn right now. Yes, I can prototype in code with my real design system components; I enjoy it, and I still want to be on a canvas some of the time. That is where I nudge things quickly, pull a screen apart, see the whole flow and its hierarchy at a glance, put three versions side by side, and pull someone over to argue about them. And at times, the prompt, wait, watch, prompt again loop bores me enormously. Sometimes it is real speed, and sometimes it is waiting that only looks like speed. And I want to use the right thing at the right time.

It is not nostalgia; it is about the outcome. And it seems I am not alone: in a Stanford study, designers who laid out several versions side by side made better work than those who improved one version at a time: more clicks when the ads ran live, higher scores from experts, more varied ideas. This study is from before AI; however, a prompt box clearly works like the second group: one screen, then a better version of it.

Good products come from comparing, not only refining, and a canvas is still the cheapest place to do so. If you only work in code, that is absolutely fine. But with a clean system, you do not have to give up the canvas to get there: the same components can live on both. And if your system cannot be mirrored onto a canvas at all, that is worth a closer look, because it usually says more about the system than about the canvas.

The good news is that I no longer have to choose. A screen I prototype in code becomes real library components in Figma; I pull it apart on the canvas, try versions, and send it back without anyone redrawing a thing.

This is what I call In-System Design: for every task you pick the surface that does the best job, and you never leave the system to get there. Code or canvas up to you.

This article shows how, step by step, and what the round trip keeps catching along the way.

I also ran through this workflow in the AI&Design System Jam Session by TJ Pitre, Ian & Brad Frost:

The one condition: same names, same properties

A prototype can only travel if every element points at the real component on both sides. In my setup, the code is the source of truth, so the Figma component carries the code’s exact name and properties: Button, with a variant that is primary, secondary, ghost or danger. Same spelling, same lowercase, no “Style: Filled”. I call this In-System Design: designing with the system’s real parts, on whichever surface suits the question.

With that in place, moving a screen is a lookup, not a translation. A ghost button on the canvas is <Button variant="ghost"> in code. When I had an agent rebuild a booking flow from Storybook in Figma, it placed 21 library components without making a single visual decision. If the names do not match (Figma says Size = Medium, code says size="md"), someone has to interpret, and an AI interprets with great confidence.

I have stopped worrying about tiny pixel differences. Figma and CSS will never agree on every stroke, and the final look happens in code anyway. A green button where the system says blue is a different matter, and that is what the checks are for.

Start anywhere, stay in the system

In-System Design means I can start wherever the question is. Think of the AI as a hub in the middle, connected to the code on one side and Figma on the other, with everything aligned, and you tell it where to build first. “Build me an onboarding flow in code with our design system” works, and so does the same request in Figma. Wherever you start, if you need the other side, you tell the AI to place it there, and back again. As long as you stay in the system, it does not matter where you begin.

The AI sits in the middle, with one arm in the code and one in Figma. Same components on both sides, so it does not matter where you start.

This article covers the two workflows that involve the canvas: the full round trip from code to Figma and back or the other way around, and what you can do if you only have the Figma side. (To prototype in code alone with your real design system, you need to set it up first; I explain this in Part 2.)

1. From code prototype to Figma and back

What you need:

  1. A Figma library that matches your code exactly in names and properties, published. I explain how to build one with MCP in part 1.
  2. A prototype file: a new, empty Figma file with that library connected under Assets.
  3. An MCP connection to the Figma prototyping file, the standard plug that lets an AI work inside Figma. I use Figma Console MCP by Southleft and recommend it for this kind of work.
  4. And an AI agent, not only a chat. A chat only sees what you paste into it. An agent can open your project, run Storybook and work in Figma for you: for example, the Code tab in the Claude desktop app (that is Claude Code, which I use), Codex, Cursor or similar
  5. A way to prototype in code with your real components: either a custom design system MCP your developers built, or the Storybook MCP as I showed in Part 2
  6. Access to the codebase on a design branch, a safe copy of the code where you cannot break anything, and where prototypes in code are picked up from and sent back to (more on that below).

From Code to Figma

I use the Storybook MCP for prototyping. My Storybook has a Prototypes section with a course sign-up page prototype I made by connecting it to Claude and asking it to set this up: real components, clickable, running on my laptop.

In my example, the top bar is not a component because my sample system is deliberately small and not ready yet. So I expect to see the same in Figma: All components and a suggested top bar.

Figma file open, library connected, MCP on. Now I tell Claude, my hub in the middle, what I want. I mostly use voice, so my prompts are a bit chatty; once your workflow is set, most of this ends up in a skill:

In my Storybook there is a prototype called Course sign-up. Send it over to the open Figma file called Prototype. Rebuild it with my Figma components, set up exactly the same way as you see it in code. Add comments to the prototype for anything I need to know, and put a little note next to it: components you could not build, gaps, anything else I should know.

What comes back is the flow as Figma screens, connected as a clickable prototype, with comments where Figma cannot show the behaviour.

The note it leaves for me

You might have noticed I ask for a little note beside the prototype, and this part is crucial. It lists the components it used, what it built by hand (no top bar component, so it assembled one and said so), the gaps, and suggestions, like turning that top bar into a proper component. I read that note before I look at the screens, and you can shape it to whatever your team needs to know.

My favourite: check that the components are real

Now my favourite shortcut of the whole project: press Cmd+Y (Ctrl+Y on Windows). It switches Figma to the wireframe view, and every instance of a library component shows up in purple, while anything drawn by hand does not. It became my new best friend, because in one second I can see whether I am looking at my system or at a drawing of it. Every library component shows purple; the top bar and plain layout frames don’t, and the note lists them correctly.

From here it is design work, and this is the bit I love: change text, move things, put three versions next to each other, try a completely different layout, make notes, discuss it with the team. My library is connected and matches the code, so anything I add from it is the real thing too.

From Figma back to code

Then back to code, as all components and props match, it can simply be picked up in Storybook:

Have a look at the Course sign-up prototype in the open Figma file and bring it back into Storybook, updating the prototype in code. Use only components from the system, and show me anything you would have to make up before you write it.

On the way back, the AI reads every instance by the library component it comes from and the props that are set, not by its layer name. Anything that is not a library instance gets listed instead of quietly rebuilt. When I composed a booking tour in Figma from library instances and sent it to code, it came back exactly as designed.

What the trip catches on the way

I expected the round trip to save time. I did not expect it to find bugs, and it keeps finding them, because every crossing is a second pair of eyes on the system.

  • Twenty-one pixels. I sent a sign-up page to Figma, and the Figma screen came out 21 pixels shorter than the one in Storybook. My first thought was “Figma is off again”. It was the code: two form components wrapped their help text in a paragraph that kept the browser’s default margin, and every automated check had waved it through, because it broke no rule. The Figma components had the spacing as intended, so the copy caught the original.
  • Figma changing the flow, rightly. My Figma dialog had no slot, so a form could not sit inside it. Instead of hacking around it, the flow changed: the form became its own step and the dialog only confirms. The code kept that, so both stayed one design.
  • A bad habit, faithfully copied. A top bar used an empty spacer layer to push things apart, because the code did, in three pasted copies. In code, nobody had noticed. On a canvas, an empty layer looks like what it is and could be fixed.

2. What if I do not have all of this? Prototyping in Figma, pointing at code

No code playground yet, no design branch, no Storybook MCP? No worries; this is the case for most teams right now, as design systems aren’t AI-ready overnight. You can still do the canvas half, and this one surprises people most: you can prototype directly in Figma with AI and still hand over something a developer reads as real components.

What you need: points 1 to 4 from the list above. A matching, published library, an empty prototype file with that library connected, the MCP into Figma, and an agent.

I have an empty Figma file open called Prototype, and the MCP is on. Create a prototype of a blog page, plus a detail page for an article that opens when I click one of the blog articles. Use the connected library for everything you need and always use my existing components. Only if you absolutely cannot find something, create it, and tell me. Put a little note beside the prototype: which components you used, anything I should know, any gaps or problems, and anything you had to make up.

In-System means all stations are optional add-ons. You pick and work with what you have or need.

Same habits as above: read the note, press Cmd+Y, then design and you get a pretty decent prototype. If your naming is aligned and you hand this off, it’s probably easier to rebuild than vibe-coded chaos, plus as soon as you can start prototyping with your design system in code, this clicks in nicely.

What if the AI invents a new component in Figma?

In my setup, it hasn’t happened yet because I tell it to use only the connected library and to show me anything it has to make up, but still, working with AI, it loooves to give you extras you never asked for. So even if it did, it would happen in the prototype file, which is the only file the MCP works in. The main library the whole team designs with never gets touched, which makes the setup an accidental drift blocker.

Fun fact: so far, the biggest source of errors has not been the AI at all. It has been library updates I forgot to accept in the prototype file, so the AI built with last week’s components. Publish, accept, then prompt.

And when the code side is ready later, these screens can go into code the same way as above.

My prototyping skill, and what I improved along the way

A disclaimer first, because it matters: none of this is an established workflow. It is very new and still trial and error, on my side too.

After typing the same instructions a third time, I turned them into a skill: a packaged set of instructions the AI loads automatically when that job comes up. Now I say “use the skill to send the prototype from Storybook to Figma” and it runs through its steps. You can ask Claude to show and summarise a skill for you, then make it your own.

The improvements that made the biggest difference:

  1. Gaps are marked in the Figma layer itself, not only in a note. A missing navigation becomes a layer with GAP in its name (an emoji works too, if you like it louder), so it can never be mistaken for a real component later.
  2. A Figma manifest. I took this idea from watching developers build custom MCPs for their design systems. They give the AI a small JSON file listing what exists, so it does not have to crawl through all the code every time, and I thought, why not do the same for Figma? My Figma manifest lists every library component with its properties, plus the internal key Figma needs to place it (the name says what to place, the key is the handle to pick it up with). Before I had it, one rebuild spent most of its effort digging through the whole library listing, about 59,000 characters, to find a single text style. Now that is a lookup of a few lines. It turned out to be the biggest speed difference of all, and it doubles as the check that Figma still matches the code.
  3. Layout names from code. Components are the furniture; layout is the arrangement. My codebase has a small vocabulary for arranging things: stack, cluster, split, columns, grid and page. Figma has auto layout but no names for arrangements, so every frame ends up as “Frame 47” and comes back into code as a guess. Now the skill reads the layout file from the code before it builds, and names my auto-layout frames the same way, with every gap bound to a spacing variable. Not perfect, but a developer recognises the structure instead of translating it. If that sounds alien, remember it the day you and your team run into layout problems; it might spark a better idea.
  4. Notes on the canvas, always in the same shape. Four headings: ✅ real library components, 🟠 built by hand, 🔴 where Figma does not match Storybook, 💡 components worth suggesting. The 💡 list is a backlog that writes itself. My top bar has been built by hand in every single prototype, which is the system politely asking for one.
  5. And the GAPS.md, the file where every difference between Figma and code gets written down, which I explained in the first article.

The usual word of caution, since a skill can run code on your machine: read it before you install it, or have a developer look first. Mine are public if you want to have a look: storybook-figma-sync for prototyping and figma-library-from-code for the library.

The design branch: a playground away from production

All of this happens somewhere safe. In a good setup, developers create a design branch for designers (I first heard this idea from TJ Pitre): a parallel copy of the codebase where you can prototype in code, send it to Figma, design freely there and bring it back, and none of it can touch the real product. Broken states are fine, half-finished ideas are fine.

There is still a handoff, and not a minor one

The design branch is never merged into the system. It is a source of decisions, not of code. When a prototype is accepted, a developer rebuilds the accepted parts properly on a fresh branch, and the team’s checks run on every change before a person approves it. I go through those steps in in detail in part 2, it is the same process

So why bother, if it gets rebuilt anyway? Because most of the work is already done. Nobody has to negotiate what a button is or which variant it uses, so a developer transcribes decisions instead of reverse-engineering a picture. What is left are the real decisions, and the gaps are where they sit: that hand-built top bar is not a detail to tidy up, it is a new component the team has to decide on, design and build, then mirror in Figma so the next prototype can use it.

Get started: As a designer, I need three things

If you are expected to prototype with AI, this is the list I would take to your team, out loud, in a meeting:

  1. An AI-ready, context-based design system. Clean, semantic, with the context an AI needs. If it is not there yet, is someone working on it, and is everyone aware there will be gaps?
  2. A prototyping MCP that is AI-ready. Built in-house by your developers, or the Storybook MCP, which is the same idea built for you.
  3. A design branch away from production. Access to the real code, somewhere you cannot break anything.

Then the softer list, which is the harder one. The dev team has to know this is happening and set it up. Design and UX need onboarding into the code side: which branch, what is off limits, how a pull request works here. The shift in workflow, and in heads, takes time and is very much underestimated. And leadership needs to understand that scalable AI has no quick-fix builder.

A note for developers, with a lot of respect: none of this works without engineering that designers never see. What helps more than any tool is half an hour showing a designer the branch, and how you check what they hand you.

What this does not solve

  • Figma still cannot show behaviour. Error states, loading, and what happens when a request fails live in code; on the canvas, they are annotations. Good enough for a prototype, and a gap all the same.
  • It is only as current as the mirror. If the Figma library has drifted from the code, the prototype carries that with it, which is why I check sync before I build anything. My check runs as a status page in Storybook, and part 1 explains how it works.
  • Matching names is not owning the API. A button’s text is called children in both places, but in Figma it accepts words and in code it accepts anything, an icon or a spinner included. Somebody has to decide what a property may hold, and in my system that decision is still open.
  • Connections drop. Start Storybook before you start the AI session, and keep screenshots handy.
  • Not checked yet: dark mode and narrow screens on the round trip.
  • It needs a system worth prototyping with. A messy library gives you messy prototypes, only faster.

Wherever I think best

I get asked in almost every session whether designers should move into code now. The question I find more useful is whether the screen in front of you is made of your system. That one has an answer you can check, Cmd+Y on one side and the component list on the other, and it does not care where you happen to be sitting.

For me this was never about Figma or code. It is about using whichever medium fits the question that day, so I can make the best product I can, knowing that whatever I decide counts in both places. Some days that is a prompt in Storybook. Most days it is three versions next to each other on a canvas and a long conversation about which one is right, and picking the right one is still the job. That is what In-System Design means to me: fewer strong opinions about one workflow, more products that hold together.

📖 Words in this article

  • Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the code itself.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it. The
  • Storybook MCP lets it read your component list; Figma Console MCP (by Southleft) lets it build in Figma.
  • Props: the options a component has in code (size, variant, disabled). Figma calls them component properties.
  • Instance (Figma): a copy of a library component that stays linked to it.
  • Manifest: a list of every component with its properties and defaults, generated rather than written. My Figma manifest is the same for the Figma library, plus each component’s key.
  • Branch: a parallel copy of the codebase. The design branch is set aside for design, never merged into the real product.
  • Deterministic check: a check that gives the same answer every time, with no AI involved, like a test or a contrast check.
  • Layout words (from my codebase, not a standard): stack, cluster, split, columns, grid, page. Names for how components are arranged, used for Figma frames and code alike.
  • GAPS.md (my term): the file where every difference between Figma and code gets written down
  • Skill: a packaged set of instructions an AI loads by itself for a recurring job. Read one before you install it.
  • Pull request: a formal proposal to change the real product, reviewed before it is accepted.
  • In-System Design (my term): designing with the system’s real components, on whichever surface suits the question, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

title: AI Prototyping inside your design system. A hands-on guide for design & product teams.
text:
AI Prototyping inside your design system. A hands-on guide for design & product teams.

In-System Design

Why builders hand you a lookalike, what has to exist before an agent can use your components, and the MCP setup I use.

Prototyping in code is what designers do now, at least according to LinkedIn. I tried it, and after two days I wanted to throw my laptop into the sea. Good news: I came out with a process I actually like, and that works, and that is what this article is. So here is what happened:

It started with every team I worked with suddenly turning up with the same frustration. They had connected their design system to an AI builder, described a screen, and got back something that looked finished. Leadership loved it. Then a developer opened the code, said something unrepeatable, and rebuilt it from scratch with the actual design system.

I did not understand it either at first. It was connected to the real design system, so what was wrong? So I started poking around the code, comparing it to the original.

The answer sits in the code, and that is the whole problem. Developers see it in a glance and are quietly furious: why are you handing me this? Everyone else sees a screen that works: looks fine, just ship it. Both are right; neither can explain it to the other, and this is how I ended up in my favourite workshops again: translating between the two.

This gap is not just awkward; it is expensive. Plans get made as if the AI prototype were most of the work, dates get promised on it, and then the rebuild happens quietly under pressure, while capable people work late to keep up with a speed AI promised, not understanding what went wrong and trying to fix it with more DESIGN.md files.

It happens often enough to have a name. Writing in Forbes, Yunhao Jiao calls it the prototype wall: excitement in week one, concerns around week three, abandonment by month two.

Before the solution (and yes, there is one, actually more than one), a quick look at what is actually going on. It takes a minute, and I know you want to skip ahead, but don’t; it helps you tell whether the next prototyping product you launch is useful when you work in a design system.

Why ready-made AI builders will not give you the output you need when working with a design system

The Lovables, Bolts and Claude Designs of this world all have a little button that says connect your design system. Not false advertising; that would be harsh, and nobody is trying to trick anyone (who would do that in tech and AI?!). They do read your design system indeed, then build their own version of it, usually (but not all) on shadcn and Tailwind.

The first screen looks close. The more you prompt, the more it invents, and nothing that comes out points at your real components. Totally fine for a quick idea, but useless for something you have to build and maintain inside a design system to scale and ship. Different tools for different jobs.

Prompting harder will not fix it, and neither will another markdown file. The problem is not the instructions. The components are not real.

I started writing a breakdown of each builder, got halfway, and realised it will be out of date by the time you read it. So, two prompts instead.

Ask the builder, after it has generated a screen:

Show me the code for the primary button on this screen. Which file is that component imported from, and which props did you set? Do not change anything. Compare it to my original design system button and show me similarities or differences.

Or ask an AI to read the docs for you:

Read the official documentation for [tool]. Using only the docs, with quotes and links: when I connect my design system, does it install my component package and use my components with their props, or does it copy and rebuild them? Where does the generated code live, and how do I get it out?

Example: Claude Design.
I have to admit Claude Design surprised me; it does a better job than I expected. However, let’s look at the details because it is still (and this might change rapidly) not what we need: The marketing says it builds with your real design system components and checks its output against your system. The setup docs say Claude “extracts” them from whatever you give it: a codebase, design files, even slide decks. Those are two different sentences, so I gave it my own repo to prototype with and had a closer look at our all-time favourite component: the button.

Every prop, value and default came back right, and my CSS came with it, every token name intact, no invented colours. But Base UI had been dropped for its own helpers, my scoped classes had become global copies, and the types were gone. Its own handover note says it plainly: “This is a recreation for design and prototyping.” A very good copy, frozen the day it was made, that a developer cannot simply merge.

📌 Note, 26 October 2026. Claude Design moves into Claude in December, and their setup already flags the Claude Code route as the higher-fidelity one for React. So this recreation step may quietly disappear. Run the prompt above and you will know before I do.

What you actually need: a component list and an MCP

The difference isn’t a better prompt. It is two pieces: a list of what your design system really contains, and a connection the agent can ask through.

A list to pick components from: the manifest

A component in code is correct, complete and something you would have to read line by line to work out what it offers. A designer gives up halfway, and an agent burns through its budget wading through thousands of files doing the same.

What an agent needs instead is the component as a list. One entry per component: its name, what it is for, every property, every allowed value, every default. Write it once, generate it from the code, and add nothing. In most setups, that file is JSON and it is called a manifest, and it looks a bit like this:

Read it the way the agent does: there is a Button; it is the primary action trigger; it comes in four variants and three sizes; and unless told otherwise, it is primary and medium. That list has no room for a fifth variant.

Three things worth knowing about it:

  • It is generated, not written. Storybook, for example, produces one from your stories and your component types. A script can write one. A custom setup usually keeps a richer version with tokens and patterns alongside the components.
  • It is not documentation and not a design file. It is the facts, written once, so nobody has to interpret them. A very boring inventory list.
  • It is yours. Any agent can read it, so it does not tie you to one tool. More important than you might think.
And it is why everything else becomes possible: the agent picks instead of inventing; it is cheap to read compared with a whole repository; checks become possible because there is something to compare against; and gaps become visible because anything that cannot go in the list becomes a conversation.

No list, no AI prototyping, however good your components are.

The connection: MCP, so the agent asks instead of remembering

The list has to be reachable while the agent works, and the standard for that is MCP, the Model Context Protocol: the plug that connects your design system, so the agent can ask what exists instead of guessing. You may know it from the Figma MCP, which lets an AI read your Figma file directly. In Claude, these are called connectors, same thing.

Without it, an agent answers from memory, and it has seen thousands of design systems, so you get the most common version of a button, with bits of yours mixed in. With it, every answer comes from your system, in this session.

Why it holds: no step trusts the one before it

Five things have to happen in a solid setup, and none of them is visible to you:

  1. Look it up, do not remember. Every session starts by asking the system what exists today. A model’s memory of your Button is the one thing you can be sure is out of date.
  2. Choose, do not invent. The agent composes from a closed list: these components, these values, these tokens. Nothing in the prompt should be able to add a fifth variant.
  3. Check against the system, not against taste. Automatically, before a human looks: are these real components, real tokens, does it meet the rules your team wrote down.
  4. Look at the rendered thing. Code that parses is not UI that works, and neither of you can tell from the code alone.
  5. A person decides. Everything green means the machine found nothing. It does not mean the work is good.

Two ways to get one

For prototyping with your own system in code, there are currently two realistic routes (check the date; this stuff moves fast). Both are built by developers. Your job is to know which one to ask for and what it costs them.

(There is a third, on the canvas side, where you prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code. Figma clicks into this far more smoothly than most people think, and it gets its own article, part 3 of this series, on 10 November 2026.)

Wait, can’t I just send the agent straight into the code?

In a small system, yes. My own website has a handful of components, and setting all of this up there was overkill. In a real system it breaks in two ways. The first is noise: the agent wades through thousands of files, internal helpers and types, which is slow and expensive. Storybook’s own test found its MCP used 27% fewer tokens and finished almost three times faster. The second is drift: code shows what exists, not what was intended. A product repo holds every old version, every one-off and every hand-built copy, and an agent copies whatever it finds most of, so the drift spreads. The MCP answers only with what the system sanctions. A custom one adds what code can’t say at all: the patterns your team agreed on and the rules that check them.

Where exactly the line sits, I don’t know, and I haven’t seen anyone put a number on it. The signs are easier to spot: the agent rebuilds a component that already exists, copies an old pattern instead of the current one, or sessions get noticeably slower and pricier. If you’ve found where that point is for your team, I’d be happy to hear it. Till then let’s have a look at our option and you just give it a go:

1. The Storybook MCP, the quick and easy route.

Most design systems already have a Storybook, which is why I start here with teams.

In case you have not met it: Storybook is a website that shows every component in your codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the code itself, with a small stories file next to each component listing its examples, so what you click through is built from the real thing.

That part you probably already have. The Storybook MCP add-on is what lets an agent use it too: it passes your component list over, so you prompt and get a prototype made of real components. Most of what I described above comes with it, the list, the preview, running your tests, and even the wording for your rules file, since the docs hand you a snippet that tells your agent never to invent a property. What does not come with it are the gates at the end, which stay with your team’s checks.

Normally your developers set this up once and give you a branch to prototype on, and that is the version I would ask for. You can also do it yourself, which is what I did. Start on a playground design system rather than the real product: I keep a small one for trainings, and any little open-source system works too. If it has no Storybook yet, that is fine, your agent can add one.

One thing to sort out first: you need an agent that works inside your project, like Claude Code or Codex. What that means in practice is that a design system is a folder of files. You download it, you open that folder with Claude Code, and from then on the AI can read those files, change them and start things up on your machine. A chat window only ever sees what you paste into it.

Then give your agent this:

Set up the Storybook MCP in this repo, following the official docs at https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai/mcp/overview. Install the add-on, switch on the components manifest, add the MCP server to my agent, and paste the agent instructions snippet from the docs into my agent’s rules file, whichever one this project uses. Then verify by listing all documented components, and tell me what you changed and anything you could not do.

What it needs: Storybook 10 or newer (it will tell you if you do not have it, and the prompt above updates it), the components manifest switched on since it is off by default, and either a branch you are allowed to work on, which your dev team sets up, or a local playground folder you connect to. After that the agent can see your components and their guidelines, find and write stories, show you a preview, and run your tests.

Using the Storybook MCP to prototype

Point your agent at the folder or branch you are allowed to work in, then ask it to open Storybook. It starts on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001, which is a website only you can see. Nothing is published, nothing leaves your laptop, and you can close it again by stopping it.

Then I just talk to it:

Using the Storybook MCP, make a separate section for prototyping, and create my first prototype: a sign-in and a register page. Use only components from my system. If something does not exist, piece it together from what is there, mark it clearly, and tell me what you had to invent.

A minute later there is a prototyping section in my Storybook with a page made of real components, clickable, running locally.

📌 Tip: I always ask for a short list underneath of what it used and what it had to make up. I still do “need” to invent here and there, but I need to know.

That is the whole experience from where I sit. A prompt and a result, with all the machinery out of sight, and something to hand over that makes sense to a developer.

Add a skill long term
By the third run you will be typing the same corrections. That is the moment for a skill: a packaged set of instructions your agent loads automatically for this job. Mine says which components may be used, how to mark anything invented, and what to write underneath. One safety note, since a skill can run code on your machine: install them from people you trust, or have a developer look first.

2. A custom design system MCP, the serious route

What a team with engineers builds for its own system, and where the best results come from, because everything in it is shaped around what that system actually holds.

The gist is always the same. A server answers from machine-readable files about the system: every component with its real properties, every token, and the compositions the team has agreed are the right way to build a pattern. The agent has to query that before it writes anything, the generated code gets checked back against the same files, rendered so somebody can look at it, reviewed by you, and run through the team’s automated checks before anything merges.

Beyond that they differ a lot, and the ones I have seen vary in what they hold, how strict they are, and where the checks sit. Brad Frost was kind enough to give me a tour of his, which goes by the name Eddie, and it was quietly mad: I had a conversation with it and watched a page assemble itself in front of me, theme changes and all, in something that is not a chat window. I later worked through the course he runs with Ian Frost and TJ Pitre (no advert; it just truly helped me), which is where the pieces finally clicked for me. I am building a small MCP for my own products and for teaching now, from the design side rather than the engineering one, enjoying it more than I expected and learning a ton.

Another interesting read about building custom prototyping tools with AI is this one by Atlassian, published in November 2025

Using a custom design system MCP

You still point your agent at a branch and describe a screen. And this is the experience you should have working with it.

The difference is what happens out of sight: it asks a system built for exactly this, so it knows your patterns as well as your components; it knows which combinations your team has blessed, and it follows your rules rather than a generic snippet. You notice it in the small things: fewer corrections, fewer invented layouts, and a gaps list that is about your product instead of about the tooling. The one I saw was also significantly faster, close to real time at times. The cost is that somebody has to build and keep it, which is why it belongs to teams who ship a system rather than to one designer with a playground.

Which one to ask for

  • No Storybook, no engineers to spare: fix that first. Nothing here works without a component list, and Storybook is the cheapest way to get one.
  • Small teams, Storybook already there: ask for the MCP add-on, the manifest switched on, and a branch to work on. An afternoon of developer time.
  • Enterprise with a design system team: they will most likely build a custom MCP, because they can staff it. More power, and more governance to agree before anything moves.
  • Nothing is ready: do not reach for a builder to fill the gap. Clean up what you have, and prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code until the code side catches up.

Either way, this infrastructure is development work. What a designer can do is ask for the right three things: a component list, a connection, and branch access.

Oh no, but I already have so much vibe-coded work!

In the long run, I recommend one of these approaches outlined above; however, there is a really fun Skill by called vibe killer by Brad Frost that gets all your vibed mess back into the system. I haven’t personally used it in a real setup yet, but go for it and tell me how it went. It looks very promising, and I love the name.

Handing off an AI prototype

The prototype still gets rebuilt, and knowing what happens next changes how you build it.

In a decent setup, you work on a design branch (it could be called anything; I took the naming from this article by TJ Pitre, as it makes a lot of sense) and hand over what you built. The design branch itself is never merged. Accepted ideas are rebuilt on a feature branch, and that is where the pull request happens: a formal way of saying, come and look at this before it goes in.

Then: developers add what a prototype does not have: real data, loading, errors, empty states. Then come the automated checks that run on every proposed change, which is what people mean when they say CI: tests, accessibility, responsiveness, whether everything used is a real component, and performance. Some teams add an AI eval that reads the change and asks whether it follows the rules and does what the ticket asked. Then a person approves it, because a green build is not a yes. It runs through all of this stuff; you don’t need to know the details, but you need to know it is there.

So why bother, if it gets checked and partly rebuilt anyway? Because the rebuild is cheap when the parts already exist. A developer transcribes decisions instead of reverse-engineering a picture.

Also, you find out now, while it is still a prototype, whether the system can express what you designed. And the thing you hand over behaves, so you can test it with people instead of asking them to imagine a click.

If you get the chance, ask your developers to show you what their checks do with your prototype. One session of that will teach you more than a year of handover templates.

📌 Tip: this is the step your prototype walks into, and somebody has already automated it. Brad Frost has published skills that carry a finished Storybook page into the product’s codebase and all the way to a pull request, with a build, a side-by-side comparison and accessibility checks on the way. Send it to your developers, and read it yourself: it spells out what a careful handover actually involves, which is useful the next time somebody tells you the prototype is basically done.

What this does not solve

  • It needs a system worth prototyping with. Messy components produce tidy-looking nonsense.
  • It does not tell you what to build. Perfect components plus no knowledge of your users gives you consistent, average screens.
  • It is not production code, however real it looks.
  • There is no established workflow yet, mine included. This is a few months of my own trial and error, and the parts I would bet on are the component list and the checks, not my exact prompts.
  • Both sides, design and dev, have to move. Designers need to get near a codebase, which starts with asking for access. Developers need to make the system readable and open the door. Neither is a tooling problem.

And the canvas? Very much alive

Remember the laptop I wanted to throw into the sea? Everything above fixes most of that, not all of it. Prototyping in code is useful, and handing over in code matters more than ever, but I still do my best thinking on a canvas, with several versions next to each other and notes beside them.

Ditching Figma has become a sort of credential this year, and I have yet to see a link between how loudly a tool gets declared dead and the quality of what ships. Figma is also moving: it has shown something called Code Sources, still in closed beta, which would let a Figma file point at the real components in a codebase instead of at a copy of them (neither Make nor Code Layers do that today). And now you know what that means! If it ships the way it was demoed, a good part of what I do by hand disappears. Nothing here depends on it, and it is the release I am watching most closely.

Until then, I do not have to choose. When your Figma library mirrors the code, the same agent works on both sides, and a prototype can move between them made of the same real components. I want to work where the work is best done, wherever the job needs me that day, and I call that In-System Design. The canvas half of it is part 3 of this series, out on 10 November 2026.

The custom MCP thinking in this article owes a lot to Brad Frost, Ian Frost and TJ Pitre’s course.
The Storybook details come from their MCP documentation.

📖 Words in this article

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it.
  • Manifest: the component as a list. Every property, allowed value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, switched on in its config.
  • Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.
  • Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code.
  • Props: the options a component has in code (size, variant, disabled). Figma calls them component properties.
  • Design branch: a parallel copy of the codebase that developers set up for designers. Nothing you do there can reach the product. I read this idea first in an article by TJ Pitre.
  • Pull request: a formal proposal to change the real product, reviewed before it is accepted.
  • CI (continuous integration): checks that run automatically on every proposed change.
  • Eval: an AI reading the work and judging it against a standard. Useful, not deterministic.
  • Skill: a packaged set of instructions an agent loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.
  • In-System Design (my term): designing with the real components of the system, on whichever surface the task needs, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

title: Every new medium gets called cheating
text:
Every new medium gets called cheating

How a machine I didn’t trust taught me to be bad at things again.

I was a skeptic.

Let the record show, I too, was against it.

When Ted Chiang wrote in The New Yorker that AI isn’t going to make art, I felt vindicated. I forwarded it. To people who had not asked (sorry).

His point was that art is the sum of thousands of small choices, and a machine that makes most of them for you has removed the art. I summarized this at dinners as “it’s a vending machine with ambitions,” which got an eye roll and some confused looks.

Writing is my home turf. I own about 14 favorite pens. I have opinions about semicolons. So when a machine showed up promising to write for me, I reacted the way a cat reacts to a new cat: I sat very still, judged it from across the room, and waited for it to leave.

I first got really riled up when a client called my writing “too AI” for using my dear Oxford comma and trusty em-dash. Things started feeling personal then, and they have ever since.

AI has never made a single thing I’m proud of. But it did something weirder, and honestly better. It made me brave enough to be a beginner again, in mediums I’d been too scared to touch for years.

Let me explain.

Every medium has a bouncer.

Every medium has a bouncer. It’s a feeling rather than a person. And some mediums have a friendlier door policy than others.

In a ceramics studio it’s the sense that everyone else knows where the good glaze is hidden and has agreed not to tell you. In coding it’s the suspicion that you must already know what a terminal is before you are allowed to ask what a terminal is.

The bouncer doesn’t check your talent. He checks whether you look like you belong. And for most of my adult life, I have walked up to the door of some new medium, made eye contact with him, said “never mind, I’m a writer,/designer/not-this” and gone home.

Why? Well, imposter syndrome. It took me roughly 35 years to accept that, no matter the success, we all feel it.

I made a very active effort to convert myself.

AI actually played a bigger role in it than I’d like to admit. And yet I’m admitting it here because it was not the obvious — the machine making anything for me. It was that I could finally ask the stupid question. At eleven at night. Forty times in a row. Without anyone sighing, checking their phone, or saying “well, it’s pretty basic.” This made the much-dreaded learning curve suddenly feel totally in my control, on my own terms, and more like a fun slip-and-slide rather than Sisyphus’ hill.

So…for example…how do you write a truly three-dimensional character? What is a web repo? And what am I not getting about Picasso?

Three questions. Three mediums. Old me would have needed a writing course, a very patient developer friend, and maybe an art history degree.

New me needed one evening and zero dignity.

And it’s not just me feeling brave btw. When researchers from Stanford and MIT gave an AI assistant to more than 5,000 customer support agents, the newest, least experienced people got 34% more done per hour. The veterans? Barely changed. The researchers’ explanation: the tool passes along what experienced people know and helps newcomers move down the learning curve faster.

Translation: AI is kind of wasted on experts and a gift to beginners. And in every new medium, guess who’s the beginner?

The gatekeeping, it turned out, was mostly mine. I had been running the door on myself.

A brief history of reply guys.

It comforts me that we have been here before. Many, many times. Actually.

Around 370 BC, Plato wrote down Socrates complaining that writing would make people forgetful and give them the look of wisdom without the real thing. Writing. My home turf. The very first AI panic was about my favorite pen. (And yes, we only know Socrates hated writing because someone wrote it down.)

In 1492, a fellow German, the abbot Johannes Trithemius, wrote In Praise of Scribes, a passionate case that monks should keep copying books by hand because the printing press would make them lazy. Then he had it printed. What a diva was he? Iconic.

Then, in 1859, reviewing the Paris Salon, the poet Charles Baudelaire, and my second favorite poet with the initials CB, announced that photography was where untalented, lazy painters went to hide. He loved ragebait. If he’d had a comments section, he would have lived in it for sure.

Around the same time, the painter Paul Delaroche reportedly declared that painting was dead. Painting has now been dead for roughly 165 years and is doing great. It has gallery representation. It has a podcast. It probably has a trust fund.

Photography, meanwhile, became a medium in its own right, with its own geniuses and its own snobs who now say the same things about phones.

That is the pattern. History repeating herself.

Every new medium gets called cheating by the people who are good at the old one. I know this because I was one of them (remember that article I forwarded?).

But I broke that generational trauma.

Because here’s what the reply guys always miss: the tools that made a medium easier never kill it. They crack it open. And yeah, that is kinda scary. Mostly, if you’re an insecure dude, I guess?

Before 1841, painters stored their oil paint in pig bladders tied with string. Then a broke American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented the collapsible paint tube. Suddenly paint was portable, painters walked outside, and Renoir later said that without tubes there would have been no Monet, no Cézanne, no Impressionism at all. Wild.

Anyhow, easier didn’t mean worse. Easier meant more people, in more places, painting things nobody had painted before. That’s what a lower learning curve does. It lets more people in. I’m unfortunately woke enough to think that’s a good thing.

Craft is just a conversation with your material.

The sociologist Richard Sennett describes craft as a conversation with your material. You push, it pushes back, and that resistance is what forces you to revise and, eventually, to get good.

Wood has a grain. Clay collapses when you’re impatient. Watercolor does whatever it wants and then dries in a shape that looks like a disappointed relative that puts your toddler in tears.

AI pushes back too, just in a more humiliating way.

It does exactly what you said instead of what you meant. Often cheerfully, with bullet points to really drive the point home. Ugh.

For someone who writes a lot, this is a daily performance review of my own clarity. The resistance is in the gap between the idea in my head and the sentence I typed (or spoke). That gap has a…texture. You kinda learn to feel it.

That, I’m sorry to report to my former self, is a medium.

Brian Eno wrote in his diary in 1995 that whatever feels weird and ugly about a new medium tends to become its signature.

So I look at AI’s current tics (the extra fingers, the relentless enthusiasm, the word “delve”) with new tenderness.

In twenty years someone will add them back on purpose and call it vintage. And if you know me, you know I’m a sucker for that.

Fluids take the shape of their container.

Don’t worry, I have not totally drowned myself in the Kool-Aid. There is something that keeps me from becoming one of those people who post sunrise photos captioned “the future is here.”

I’ve already ranted about this in The taste paradox, so here’s the short version. When researchers handed writers AI-generated story ideas, the stories got rated as more creative. They also got more alike. Everyone got better, and everyone got a little more the same.

I’d been calling AI a fluid medium as a compliment. I forgot what fluids do.

Water has no shape of its own. It takes the shape of whatever holds it.

The container is you.

That’s pretty poetic. I mean, unless you’d prefer Tupperware.

Your taste, your oddness, the thing you notice that nobody else does. Which is why, on my home turf, I use it to teach me stuff that helps me reach more people. In my case, that’s making social media assets and finding other creators to engage with.

A tool that makes everyone a competent writer is a threat only to writers whose main feature was competence. Lucky for me, I’ve always been more rebel than competent.

The medium it never touched.

I have been doing a lot of things I’ve always been interested in and too afraid to try, with less fear than ever. Because really, AI didn’t teach me coding. It taught me that starting from zero is survivable. And it showed me how I learn: by asking the dumb question first and making the ugly version second. That lesson doesn’t stay inside the chat window. It leaks. Into my life. Even my parenting!

So yes, I think AI is a fluid medium. And so is the courage it leaves behind. Two liquids, one glass: the tool pours you into a new medium, and the courage keeps you there. Liquid courage, minus the hangover and the text messages you regret. Win-win.

The bouncer is still standing at the door of every medium I haven’t tried yet. He just looks smaller now. Like someone I could easily body-tackle or win against in a rap battle.

The point?

Be a beginner again.

On purpose. Pick the medium you’ve always been too scared to try, the one with the meanest bouncer. Ask it the stupid question tonight. Then go make something ugly with your actual hands.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.

title: The Stunning Bravery Of The Russell Brand Survivors
text:
The Stunning Bravery Of The Russell Brand Survivors

Content warning: The following includes descriptions of rape, sexual assault and abuse that some readers may find distressing.

Shame has changed sides. For you, me and women survivors everywhere some justice has been served: the comedian Russell Brand, 51, has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for raping a 21-year-old woman and sexually assaulting three other women between 2004 and 2009. In a UK court on November 9th, he was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.  

It’s hard to believe he’s been convicted with a lengthy sentence, isn’t it? It isn’t hard to believe survivors of rape or sexual assault, and yet, as we all know, all too often the blame falls upon the rape or sexual assault victim, not the perpetrator. Data from eight major US cities — from Los Angeles and Chicago to San Francisco — shows that less than 4% of sex crimes result in convictions, according to a study conducted by NBC News. Even though Brand was found guilty, women still feared the famous media personality would be handed a lenient sentence. Fear not; Brand must serve two-thirds of the 10-year and six-month sentence before he will be eligible for parole.  

All of this happened because truly brave women survivors came forward. Over the past four weeks, a jury of eight men and four women has watched, listened and deliberated a verdict, without any CCTV footage or forensic evidence, in Southwark Crown Court. On the day of sentencing, after Brand had been found guilty, these four incredibly brave women shared their victim impact statements (it can play a crucial role in the sentence given for Brand’s convicted crimes against them). From behind a curtain, one survivor, whom Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting, shared: “I wanted to express how this crime has impacted me. I’ve been in shock and turmoil for weeks. I was extremely upset and traumatized. I didn’t have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods — scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way […] I just want to say — a leopard may change its spots, but it’s still a leopard.” 

Another survivor, whom Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting in 2005, had her court statement read for her by the prosecution, one part of it read: “Over the years, hearing his [Brand’s] voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump.” In a similar vein, a survivor whom Brand was convicted of anally raping in 2009 said in her court statement read by the prosecution: “I am living with trauma and something I carry every day,” sharing that she had to take time away from work, move back in with her parents and she worried she’d contracted HIV. The final court statement from the fourth victim, whom Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting while working on a Channel 4 project with him in 2009, was also read for her by the prosecution, saying that following the incident she was “really upset” and felt she “lost my trust in people”. “I felt my working environment wasn’t safe,” she says, adding: “I felt powerless in that moment.” Thankfully, they’re all entitled to lifelong anonymity.  

And let’s not forget that Brand’s conviction happened because of truly brave journalists (many of whom are women). In 2023, a joint media investigation carried out by The Times and Channel 4’s Dispatches, aired the documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight. It helped to expose sexual misconduct by Brand, and subsequently, women came forward with complaints about the comedian to the police. In other words, it gave women hope. Hope they would be believed. Hope they would be listened to. Hope they will see some sort of justice.  

In his closing remarks, senior crown prosecutor David Roberts said: “Today’s result shows that fame, status, and a passage of time do not change the fundamental issue of consent. He continued by saying Brand is a “manipulative sexual predator, using his growing fame and power to create situations in which he could pursue women sexually, regardless of what they wanted, with complete disregard for the impact of his actions”. He also praised the survivors. When a sexual survivor makes an allegation, they know everything will be scrutinized about them, because for millennia shame has sat with us. Women have always been shamed for men’s wrongdoings. Today, judge Justice Bennathan made it clear shame must change sides by saying: “Whatever women wear. Wherever they go. Indeed, whatever they drink. They retain the right to say ‘no’ and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators — like you, Russell Brand — act without their consent.”  

Brand probably thought he’d be free right now. I did, too. As the Me Too movement showed, some male celebrities are never reprimanded for sexual harassment or rape. Women who feel safe enough to come forward are not believed, silenced, shut down and never see some justice. So, let me say it again for the women who made this happen: Brand has been found guilty and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison — a sentence I never thought I’d get to write. He’s a convicted rapist. But the women who came forward will never feel truly free; they’ve had to endure a prison-like hell of their own for decades after what he did to them. But their bravery has helped shame change sides, just like Gisèle Pelicot. Their bravery will be remembered, and their bravery will help other women come forward and be believed, too.
